lead: Two portraits of compassion and struggle. In the dark at the river Jabbok, Jacob wrestles with a mysterious stranger until dawn, refuses to let go until he is blessed, and leaves limping with a new name, Israel. In the Gospel Jesus sees crowds “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd”, and tells his disciples to pray for workers; in the next verse he will send them. Psalm 17 gives the hope of both: “I shall behold your face in righteousness.”

r.h: I will not let you go unless you bless me
set: After twenty years with Laban, Jacob is going home, and he learns that Esau is coming to meet him with four hundred men (32:6). He is afraid. He prays one of the great prayers of Genesis (32:9–12), sends gifts ahead, and on the last night divides his family and possessions across the ford of the Jabbok. Then he is left alone.

Background. The Hebrew carries a play on three words: the river Jabbok (yabbōq), Jacob (ya‘ăqōb), and “wrestled” (ye’ābēq). The mysterious opponent is called simply “a man”. Jacob later says he has “seen God face to face”, and the prophet Hosea speaks of the same story as a struggle with God and with the angel (Hosea 12:3–4).
str: vv. 22–24a: Jacob sends everyone across the ford and stays alone.
vv. 24b–26a: the night wrestling; the wound at the hip.
vv. 26b–29: “I will not let you go unless you bless me”; the change of name; the stranger will not give his own name.
vv. 30–32: Peniel; Jacob limps into the sunrise; the custom about the thigh muscle.
kw: The text explains the name as “you have striven with God”. Scholars note that it more likely means “God strives” or “God rules”, but the biblical explanation is what shapes the story. The people of Israel inherit a name that means struggle and blessing together.
The place where Jacob saw God’s face and lived. The next chapter returns to this when he meets Esau and says that seeing his brother’s face is “like seeing the face of God” (33:10).
Jacob’s demand. After a life of seizing a blessing by trickery, he now asks for it openly, in the dark, from one who holds it.
vv: Jacob was left alone; and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
The stranger comes when Jacob is alone and at the end of his own resources. In the Bible, encounters with God often come in such places.
I will not let you go, unless you bless me.
Wounded, Jacob will not give up. His persistence is not arrogance but need: he knows that his future depends on the blessing.
You shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with humans, and have prevailed.
A new name is a new identity. Jacob, “the heel-grabber”, becomes Israel, and the people who bear his name will carry the same story of struggle, blessing and survival.
For I have seen God face to face, and yet my life is preserved.
In the Old Testament, to see God and live is a wonder (Exodus 33:20; Judges 13:22). Jacob’s limp is the sign that the encounter was real.
ch: The Catechism says that from this account the spiritual tradition of the Church has kept a symbol of prayer as a battle of faith and as a triumph of perseverance (CCC 2573). The story does not teach that we can force God’s hand, but that God invites honest, persistent prayer from those who truly need him, and that such prayer changes the one who prays. Jacob receives both a blessing and a wound: an encounter with God leaves a mark. The Jewish custom still kept of not eating the thigh muscle (gid hanasheh) remembers this night; the Church honours Israel’s faithfulness to the memory of its own story.

set: Here ends the section of Matthew’s Gospel that shows Jesus’ works of power, chapters 8 and 9: ten miracles, as they are usually counted. Together with the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5 to 7) they show the Messiah in word and deed. The final scene is the healing of a man who could not speak, brought to Jesus by others, followed by Jesus’ summary of his whole ministry, which is almost word for word the same as 4:23. The passage prepares the sending of the Twelve in chapter 10.

Background. The crowds respond with wonder: “Never has anything like this been seen in Israel.” Some Pharisees answer with an accusation, that his power comes from the prince of demons. This charge is repeated in 12:24. Matthew’s Gospel was written when his community, Jewish believers in Jesus, was in painful disagreement with other Jewish leaders; the harsh words belong to that family argument and are not a judgment on the Jewish people.
str: vv. 32–33: the mute man speaks; the crowds are amazed.
v. 34: the accusation by some Pharisees.
v. 35: the summary: teaching, proclaiming, healing.
v. 36: Jesus’ compassion for the crowds.
vv. 37–38: the harvest and the call to pray for labourers.
kw: From splanchna, the inner organs, the seat of deep feeling. It is a word in the Gospels used almost only of Jesus (and of characters in his parables who represent God). His compassion moves him, in the body, to act.
Literally “worn out and thrown down”: people battered by life and left without anyone to lead them. The picture of the shepherdless sheep recalls Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34.
A common biblical image of God’s final gathering. The harvest here is not a threat but a promise: God’s people are ready to be gathered, and the workers are few.
vv: Never has anything like this been seen in Israel.
The crowds recognize the newness of what they see. In Matthew they speak in the name of Israel; they are not an enemy of Jesus.
he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd
Jesus sees what the crowds need before they say it. He sees them as a flock; he is the shepherd whom Israel was promised (Ezekiel 34:23).
The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few
Jesus is not complaining about the harvest but about the shortage of workers. The field is ripe; those who will gather it are few.
therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest.
The first response to need is prayer. The disciples who are told to pray are in the next verse the ones sent (10:1), so that the praying and the going belong together.
ch: The Catechism says that Christ’s compassion toward the sick and his many healings are a resplendent sign that God has visited his people (CCC 1503). The Second Vatican Council, drawing on this passage, taught that the duty of fostering vocations belongs to the whole Christian community, which must do so above all by a fully Christian life (Optatam Totius 2). That is why the Church keeps a day of prayer for vocations on the Fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday. Every Christian is both asked to pray for labourers and called to be one.

qa: Who was the man who wrestled with Jacob?

The text calls him “a man”, and Jacob concludes that he has seen God. Hosea 12:4 speaks of an angel. The story keeps the identity veiled: the opponent is God’s own messenger, speaking with God’s authority, who will not give his name (32:29). Christian readers have often seen in him a figure of God drawing close to humanity. What matters is the outcome: Jacob is blessed and renamed Israel.
study: Jacob would not let go until he was blessed. What blessing am I asking God for, and am I willing to persist in asking?
Jesus saw the crowds with compassion. Who around me looks “harassed and helpless”, and what can I do for them or pray for them?
